ai.title: Vitamin K Deficiency
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Vitamin K deficiency impairs γ‑carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X, leading to a prolonged PT and bleeding. In low‑resource settings it often follows poor diet, antibiotics, or malabsorption. Prompt recognition and replacement are essential.

sections.p: A state of inadequate vitamin K activity resulting in reduced functional clotting factors II, VII, IX and X.
b: Prolonged PT with normal aPTT (early stage)
PT > 1.5 × control or INR >1.5 in the absence of liver disease

t.b: Is the extrinsic pathway impaired? – Prolonged PT suggests vitamin K deficiency, warfarin effect or factor VII deficiency.
Quantifies PT prolongation – INR >1.5 supports deficiency when liver disease is excluded.
Confirms deficiency – often unavailable; rely on PT/INR and clinical picture.

sections.p: Severity is gauged by PT/INR magnitude and clinical bleeding.
b: Mild: PT ↑ <2 × control, no bleeding
Moderate: PT ↑ 2–3 × control or INR 1.5–3, minor bruising/petechiae
Severe: PT ↑ >3 × control or INR >3, overt bleeding (GI, intracranial)

sections.p: Identify reversible and contextual factors common in East African hospitals.
b: Nutritional deficiency – low intake of leafy greens, malnutrition
Broad‑spectrum antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone) disrupting gut flora
Malabsorption – cholestatic liver disease, cystic fibrosis, intestinal resection
Neonatal VKDB – inadequate prophylaxis, exclusive breastfeeding
Chronic kidney disease on dialysis (dialysate lacks vitamin K)
Herbal remedies containing vitamin K antagonists (e.g., cassava leaves)
Severe sepsis with DIC (overlap but PT pattern similar)

sections.p: Bleeding tendency varies from easy bruising to life‑threatening hemorrhage.
b: Easy bruising, petechiae on extremities
Bleeding from umbilical stump in neonates
Gastrointestinal bleeding – melena or hematochezia
Intracranial hemorrhage – headache, vomiting, seizures
Hematuria or epistaxis in adults

sections.p: Focus on coagulation profile and underlying causes; adapt when tests are unavailable.

t.b: Is the extrinsic pathway abnormal? – Prolonged PT confirms suspicion; if unavailable, use bedside clotting time (e.g., 20‑minute whole‑blood clot test).
Rule out thrombocytopenia – normal platelets point to coagulation factor problem.
Exclude hepatic synthesis failure – normal LFTs support isolated vitamin K deficiency.
Detect GI bleeding source – positive test guides further work‑up.
Look for intra‑abdominal bleeding or liver disease.

sections.p: Identify patients at imminent risk of fatal bleeding.
b: Intracranial hemorrhage signs – altered consciousness, focal deficits
Massive GI bleed – hemodynamic instability, melena with tachycardia
Severe postpartum hemorrhage in vitamin K‑deficient mothers
Neonatal encephalopathy from intracranial bleed

sections.p: Replace vitamin K, treat the cause, and monitor coagulation.
b: Treat underlying infection or stop offending antibiotics
Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) for active severe bleeding when vitamin K alone is insufficient
Avoid warfarin or other vitamin K antagonists until deficiency corrected

sections.p: Ensure sustained vitamin K status and monitor for recurrence.
b: Repeat PT/INR 24 h after replacement; aim for INR ≤1.2
Promote dietary sources – leafy greens, vegetable oils
Review antibiotic prescriptions; limit broad‑spectrum use
Consider weekly oral vitamin K in malnourished children where feasible

sections.p: Differential diagnoses that share prolonged PT or bleeding.
b: Warfarin toxicity – history of anticoagulant use, INR often >5
Factor VII deficiency – congenital, isolated PT prolongation from birth
Early disseminated intravascular coagulation – also raises aPTT and D‑dimer
Liver failure – both PT and aPTT prolonged, abnormal LFTs
Normal aPTT does not exclude severe deficiency; focus on PT
Mild PT prolongation may be missed if laboratory reference range is wide
Vitamin K level may be normal in acute deficiency because of redistribution

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of consciousness or seizures (possible intracranial bleed)
Rapidly expanding bruises with compartment syndrome signs

faq.q: Why is PT prolonged but aPTT often normal in vitamin K deficiency?
faq.a: Factor VII (extrinsic pathway) has the shortest half‑life, so it falls first, affecting PT; factors II, IX, X affect aPTT later.

faq.q: Can oral antibiotics cause vitamin K deficiency?
faq.a: Yes, they suppress gut bacteria that synthesize vitamin K, especially with prolonged courses.

exam: A 2‑month‑old infant presents with scalp bruising and a bulging fontanelle – what is the most likely diagnosis and immediate management? — Recognise neonatal VKDB, give IV vitamin K and arrange neuro‑imaging.
An adult on ceftriaxone for 10 days develops easy bruising and PT 22 s (control 12 s). What is the next step? — Check INR, give vitamin K1, review antibiotic necessity.

A patient with cholestatic jaundice has PT 30 s, INR 2.8, normal platelets. How do you differentiate vitamin K deficiency from liver failure? — Assess LFTs, bilirubin, albumin; if LFTs only mildly abnormal, treat as deficiency first.

During surgery you notice diffuse oozing from raw surfaces; PT is 28 s. What intra‑operative measures are appropriate? — Administer IV vitamin K, give FFP if bleeding persists, correct any hypothermia.
What are the key dietary sources of vitamin K and how can you counsel a malnourished patient? — Leafy greens (spinach, kale), vegetable oils; encourage locally available greens and fortified foods.
Why is warfarin contraindicated until vitamin K deficiency is corrected? — Warfarin further blocks γ‑carboxylation, worsening coagulopathy and raising bleeding risk.

A child on long‑term phenobarbital therapy presents with petechiae; PT is 18 s. Explain the pathophysiology. — Phenobarbital induces hepatic enzymes that increase vitamin K metabolism, lowering active vitamin K levels.
